```{python}
#| label: s2-orbit
#| include: false

# The course constants sheet, used by every figure on this page.
C, G = 2.99792458e10, 6.6732e-8
MSUN, PC, AU = 1.9891e33, 3.0856e18, 1.4959789e13
KMS, YR = 1e5, 3.156e7

# S2's published orbit: GRAVITY Collaboration 2020 (A&A 636, L5),
# Table E.1, with the mass and distance of the same fit.
S2 = dict(
    a_as=0.125058,       # semi-major axis, arcsec
    e=0.884649,          # eccentricity
    i=134.567,           # inclination, degrees
    omega=66.263,        # argument of pericenter, degrees
    Omega=228.171,       # longitude of the ascending node, degrees
    P=16.0455,           # period, years
    tp=2018.379,         # time of pericenter, year
    M=4.261e6,           # mass of Sgr A*, solar masses
    R0=8.2467,           # distance to the Galactic center, kpc
)


def s2_state(t):
    """S2's sky position (arcsec east, arcsec north of Sgr A*), its distance
    from Sgr A* (cm), its speed (cm/s) and its Newtonian radial velocity
    (cm/s, positive receding) at the times t (years), from the elements above."""
    a, e = S2["a_as"], S2["e"]
    inc, w, Om = (np.radians(S2[k]) for k in ("i", "omega", "Omega"))
    mean = 2 * np.pi * (np.asarray(t, float) - S2["tp"]) / S2["P"]
    E = mean.copy()
    for _ in range(60):                       # Kepler's equation, by Newton's method
        E -= (E - e * np.sin(E) - mean) / (1 - e * np.cos(E))
    X, Y = np.cos(E) - e, np.sqrt(1 - e**2) * np.sin(E)
    # Thiele-Innes constants: the orbit's plane turned to face us.
    A = a * (np.cos(w) * np.cos(Om) - np.sin(w) * np.sin(Om) * np.cos(inc))
    B = a * (np.cos(w) * np.sin(Om) + np.sin(w) * np.cos(Om) * np.cos(inc))
    F = a * (-np.sin(w) * np.cos(Om) - np.cos(w) * np.sin(Om) * np.cos(inc))
    Gc = a * (-np.sin(w) * np.sin(Om) + np.cos(w) * np.cos(Om) * np.cos(inc))
    north, east = A * X + F * Y, B * X + Gc * Y
    a_cm = a * S2["R0"] * 1e3 * AU             # arcsec times parsecs is AU
    M = S2["M"] * MSUN
    r = a_cm * (1 - e * np.cos(E))
    speed = np.sqrt(G * M * (2 / r - 1 / a_cm))
    nu = 2 * np.arctan2(np.sqrt(1 + e) * np.sin(E / 2), np.sqrt(1 - e) * np.cos(E / 2))
    P_s = S2["P"] * YR
    K = 2 * np.pi * a_cm * np.sin(inc) / (P_s * np.sqrt(1 - e**2))
    v_r = K * (np.cos(w + nu) + e * np.cos(w))
    return east, north, r, speed, v_r
```

At the center of the Milky Way, 26,000 light-years away, there is a dark object
four million times as massive as the Sun, and we know its mass the way we know
the Sun's: by watching things go around it. A handful of stars orbit it so
closely and so fast that in a few decades astronomers have followed one of them
all the way around, twice. This lecture is about that object, **Sagittarius
A\***, how it was weighed, why nothing but a black hole fits what was found, and
how the same star turned into the sharpest test of general relativity ever made
in a strong gravitational field. It is the black hole that lecture 4 used for
orbital precession, lecture 5 for gravitational redshift, lecture 16 for the
Event Horizon Telescope's picture and lecture 17 for the mass at the center of
the Galaxy. Here it gets a lecture of its own.

## How to read this lecture

**These notes are the reading for this lecture**; no chapter of Kutner covers
the Galactic center as it is understood today, because almost all of what
follows was measured after the book was written. The lecture builds one
argument, and it is worth holding onto from the start:

::: {.callout-important title="The idea at the center of this lecture"}
**Stars at the center of the Milky Way orbit four million solar masses packed
inside a region smaller than the Solar System. Kepler's third law weighs it,
only a black hole fits, and the same orbits show the effects general
relativity predicts.**
:::

Every tool it needs is one you already have. *Looking at the Galactic center*
says why the center has to be watched in infrared light, and how sharp the
picture has to be. *Weighing Sgr A\** turns one star's orbit into a mass with
Kepler's third law, as Newton taught us to weigh the Sun. *Why it must be a
black hole* asks what else could hold that much mass in so small a space.
*Two tests of general relativity* goes back to the precession of lecture 4 and
the redshift of lecture 5, and asks how large each one is for this star and
how they were measured.

## Looking at the Galactic center

The center of the Milky Way lies in the constellation Sagittarius, about
$8.0\ \mathrm{kpc}$ from the Sun, the value on your constants sheet: about
26,000 light-years. In 1974 radio astronomers found a tiny, bright source of
radio waves there [@balick1974], and it later took the name **Sagittarius A\***
(Sgr A\*, said "saj A star"), the star marking it out from the larger radio
source Sagittarius A around it. Everything in this lecture is about what sits
at that spot.

**It cannot be seen in visible light.** The line of sight from the Sun runs
through the disk of the Galaxy, and the dust in the disk dims visible light
from the center by tens of magnitudes, so that essentially none of it arrives;
lecture 6 met the same problem. Infrared light, with wavelengths a few times
longer, slips past dust grains much more easily, and a small but usable
fraction of it gets through. So the stars near Sgr A\* are watched in the
near infrared, at a wavelength of about $2.2\ \mu\text{m}$.

**It has to be seen very sharply.** At the distance of the Galactic center a
small angle is a large distance. The constants sheet's parallax relation,
$d\,(\mathrm{pc}) = 1/p\,('')$, says that $1\ \mathrm{AU}$ seen from
$1\ \mathrm{pc}$ spans $1''$. The size of something scales up with its
distance at a fixed angle, so

$$
s\ (\mathrm{AU}) = \theta\ ('') \times d\ (\mathrm{pc}) ,
$$ {#eq-small-angle}

and at the Galactic center, $8000\ \mathrm{pc}$ away, **one arcsecond is 8000
astronomical units**. The stars that matter here move on orbits a few
thousand astronomical units across, so their whole orbits are a fraction of an
arcsecond on the sky, and their closest approaches to Sgr A\* are thousandths
of an arcsecond.

::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: how big is S2's orbit?"}
**The question.** The star S2 moves on an ellipse whose semi-major axis spans
$0.1255''$ on the sky. How long is that semi-major axis in astronomical units
and in centimeters, taking the Galactic center to be $8.0\ \mathrm{kpc}$ away?

From @eq-small-angle, with the distance in parsecs,

$$
s = 0.1255\ ('') \times 8000\ (\mathrm{pc}) = 1004\ \mathrm{AU} .
$$

Arcseconds times parsecs gives astronomical units, which is how the parallax
relation was built. *Do the units make sense?* A length, so yes. In
centimeters,

$$
1004\ \mathrm{AU} \times \frac{1.496 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{cm}}{1\ \mathrm{AU}}
= 1.50 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm} .
$$

**About a thousand astronomical units**, some twenty-five times the size of
Pluto's orbit, and the whole ellipse, two semi-major axes long, spans only a
quarter of an arcsecond.
:::

### Sharper than the atmosphere allows

A telescope's resolution is set by diffraction, $\theta = 1.22\,\lambda/D$ (on
your constants sheet), where $D$ is the diameter of its mirror. One of the
10-meter Keck telescopes, at $2.2\ \mu\text{m}$, could in principle separate
two stars $0.055''$ apart, about $440\ \mathrm{AU}$ at the Galactic center.
**In practice the atmosphere spoils it.** Turbulent air bends starlight one
way and then another many times a second, and a star that should be a sharp
point is smeared into a blob more than ten times larger, a full arcsecond or
so. At the Galactic center, where hundreds of stars crowd into a few
arcseconds, that turns a field of stars into a glowing smudge.

**Adaptive optics** takes the smudge back out. A bright star near the target,
or an artificial star made by shining a laser up into the high atmosphere, is
watched hundreds of times a second; a computer works out how the air has
distorted it, and a thin, deformable mirror in the telescope's light path is
bent to undo the distortion before the light reaches the camera. With it, the
big telescopes reach close to their diffraction limit, and the smudge
resolves into separate stars. Take the same picture again every few months,
and you can watch the stars move.

Two groups have done exactly that since the 1990s: one led by Andrea Ghez at
UCLA with the Keck telescopes in Hawaii, and one led by Reinhard Genzel at the
Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics with the European Southern
Observatory's Very Large Telescope in Chile [@ghez2008; @gillessen2009]. Lecture
5 showed Ghez's group's animation of the orbits. Since 2016 the European group
has had a further trick, an instrument called **GRAVITY**, which combines the
light of the four $8.2\ \mathrm{m}$ telescopes of the Very Large Telescope as
an interferometer. It acts like a single telescope as large as the distance
between them, about $130\ \mathrm{m}$, sharp to a few thousandths of an
arcsecond: a few tens of astronomical units at the Galactic center.

@fig-s2-sky is the result of that monitoring for one star: the orbit of S2
(called S0-2 by the UCLA group) around Sgr A\*, drawn from the orbit the
measurements fit.

```{python}
#| label: fig-s2-sky
#| fig-cap: "The orbit of the star S2 on the sky, drawn from the orbit fitted by the GRAVITY Collaboration [@gravity2020precession]. Sgr A\\* is at the cross, at one focus of the ellipse, and the dots mark S2's position at the start of each year from 2002 to 2018, and the green diamond its closest approach to Sgr A\\*, passed in 2002 and again in 2018. The axes are offsets from Sgr A\\* in arcseconds, east to the left as astronomers draw the sky; the top and right axes are the same offsets in astronomical units at the distance of the Galactic center. The dots bunch together far from Sgr A\\*, where S2 moves slowly, and spread apart near the bottom, where it swings past Sgr A\\* in a few months, as Kepler's second law says it must."
#| fig-alt: "A chart of a tall ellipse on the sky, its long axis running nearly vertically. The horizontal axis is the east-west offset from Sgr A star in arcseconds, from plus 0.06 on the left to minus 0.075 on the right, and the vertical axis is the north-south offset, from about minus 0.02 to plus 0.18. Matching axes on the top and right give the same offsets in astronomical units, up to about 1400. An orange cross labeled Sgr A star sits just inside the bottom end of the ellipse. Blue dots mark the star's position at the start of each year from 2002 to 2018, labeled 2006, 2010 and 2014 along the way; they are spaced evenly around the top and sides and spread farther apart toward the bottom. A green diamond at the bottom of the ellipse, just below the cross and slightly to its left, is labeled closest approach, 2002 and 2018."
#| fig-height: 5.0

t_dots = np.arange(2002.0, 2018.5, 1.0)
t_line = np.linspace(S2["tp"], S2["tp"] + S2["P"], 2000)
east, north, *_ = s2_state(t_line)
ed, nd, *_ = s2_state(t_dots)
ep, npk, *_ = s2_state(np.array([S2["tp"]]))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.6, 5.0))
ax.plot(east, north, color=BLUE, lw=1.4, zorder=2)
ax.plot(ed, nd, "o", color=BLUE, ms=5, mec=INK, mew=0.5, zorder=3)
for t, x, y in zip(t_dots, ed, nd):
    if int(t) in (2006, 2010, 2014):
        ax.text(x - 0.007, y, f"{int(t)}", color=INK2, fontsize=9, va="center")
ax.plot(ep, npk, "D", color=AQUA, ms=6, mec=INK, mew=0.6, zorder=4)
ax.annotate("closest approach,\n2002 and 2018", xy=(ep[0], npk[0]),
            xytext=(0.045, 0.035), color=INK2, fontsize=9, ha="left",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=INK2, lw=0.8))
ax.plot([0], [0], "x", color=ORANGE, ms=9, mew=2, zorder=4)
ax.text(0.006, 0.006, "Sgr A*", color=ORANGE, fontsize=10, ha="left")
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_xlim(0.06, -0.075)             # east to the left, as on the sky
ax.set_xticks([0.05, 0.0, -0.05])
ax.set_xlabel(r"offset east of Sgr A* ($''$)")
ax.set_ylabel(r"offset north of Sgr A* ($''$)")
au = S2["R0"] * 1e3                   # AU per arcsecond
axt = ax.secondary_xaxis("top", functions=(lambda x: x * au, lambda s: s / au))
axt.set_xlabel("offset (AU)")
axr = ax.secondary_yaxis("right", functions=(lambda y: y * au, lambda s: s / au))
axr.set_ylabel("offset (AU)")
plt.show()
```

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-looking}

1. The Galactic center is $8.0\ \mathrm{kpc}$ away. How many light-years is
   that? How long ago did the infrared light from S2 that reaches a telescope
   tonight leave the star?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   About 26,000 light-years, so the light left S2 about 26,000 years ago.
   :::

2. What is the diffraction limit of a 10-meter Keck telescope at
   $2.2\ \mu\text{m}$, in arcseconds? What would it be in visible light, at
   $550\ \mathrm{nm}$? Explain why the sharper limit in visible light is no
   help at the Galactic center.

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   The limit is $0.055''$ at $2.2\ \mu\text{m}$, and $0.014''$ at $550\ \mathrm{nm}$. No
   visible light arrives from the Galactic center, so there is nothing to
   resolve.
   :::

3. GRAVITY works like a telescope $130\ \mathrm{m}$ across. Find its
   diffraction limit at $2.2\ \mu\text{m}$ in arcseconds, and the distance
   that angle spans at the Galactic center, in astronomical units. S2 comes
   within about $120\ \mathrm{AU}$ of Sgr A\*. Could GRAVITY tell the two
   apart at closest approach? Could a single Keck telescope?

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
   Use $\theta = 1.22\,\lambda/D$ with both lengths in the same unit, and
   convert from radians to arcseconds with the constants sheet's
   $1\ \mathrm{rad} = 206{,}265''$. Then @eq-small-angle.

   GRAVITY resolves $0.0043''$, which is $34\ \mathrm{AU}$ at the Galactic
   center, so yes. A single Keck telescope resolves about $440\ \mathrm{AU}$,
   so no: at closest approach, S2 and Sgr A\* blur together.
   :::

4. The Event Horizon Telescope's ring around Sgr A\* is about
   $52\ \mu\text{as}$ across (lecture 16), where $1\ \mu\text{as}$ is a
   millionth of an arcsecond. How many astronomical units is that, at
   $8.0\ \mathrm{kpc}$? Compare it with the size of S2's closest approach.

:::

## Weighing Sgr A\*

::: {.panel-tabset .tracks}

### Physical intuition

The way to weigh anything in astronomy is to watch something orbit it. Kepler
found that the planets obey a single rule, that the square of a planet's
period is proportional to the cube of the size of its orbit, and Newton showed
why: the rule follows from his law of gravity, and the constant of
proportionality is the mass of the Sun. **A larger mass makes the same orbit
faster.** Measure an orbit's size and how long it takes, and you have weighed
whatever it goes around, without ever seeing it.

That is all there is to weighing Sgr A\*. S2 goes around it once every
16 years, on an ellipse about a thousand astronomical units in semi-major axis
(@fig-s2-sky). Compare the Earth, which goes around the Sun once a year at one
astronomical unit. S2's orbit is a thousand times larger, so if the central
mass were the Sun's, the orbit would take $1000^{3/2}$, about 32,000, years.
It takes 16. Something must be pulling far harder than the Sun, and Kepler's
third law says how much harder: the mass at the center is about **four million
solar masses**.

Three things make this measurement unusually secure.

**It is a whole orbit, not a snapshot.** S2 was first followed in the early
1990s and passed its closest approach to Sgr A\* in 2002 [@schodel2002;
@ghez2003] and again in 2018; it has been watched all the way around, twice.
Its ellipse is not a guess at a shape from a few positions, it is a measured
closed path.

**Every star agrees.** Dozens of stars near Sgr A\* have measured orbits, of
every size and tilt, and all of them have the same point at one focus and give
the same central mass [@gillessen2009]. Whatever is there is one object, at
one point, and it does not move: Sgr A\* itself, the radio source, sits at
rest at that focus to within about a kilometer per second [@reid2020].

**The star's own mass drops out.** S2 is a hot, young star of about fifteen
solar masses. Next to four million, that is three parts in a million, far less
than the uncertainty in the measurement.

::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Think about why S2's own mass does not matter"}
Kepler's third law, in Newton's form, contains the *sum* of the two masses,
$M + m$. The pull of gravity accelerates each body in proportion to the
*other's* mass, so S2 moves in response to the four million solar masses at
the center while the center moves in response to S2's fifteen. The central
mass hardly moves at all, and S2's fifteen adds three parts in a million to
the sum. It is the same reason the planets' masses can be left out when
Kepler's law is used to weigh the Sun: Jupiter, the heaviest of them, is a
thousandth of the Sun's mass.
:::

### Mathematical explanation

**Kepler's third law**, in Newton's form, for two bodies of masses $M$ and $m$
on an orbit of semi-major axis $a$ and period $P$:

$$
P^2 = \frac{4\pi^2 a^3}{G\,(M + m)} ,
$$ {#eq-kepler}

which is on your constants sheet as $4\pi^2 R^3/G = (m_1 + m_2) P^2$. When the
orbiting body is much lighter than the central one, $m \ll M$, solve for the
central mass:

$$
M = \frac{4\pi^2 a^3}{G\,P^2} .
$$ {#eq-kepler-mass}

*Its units*: $\mathrm{cm^{3}}$ on top, and $\mathrm{cm^{3}\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}}
\times \mathrm{s^{2}} = \mathrm{cm^{3}\,g^{-1}}$ below, which leaves
$\mathrm{g}$, a mass.

**In solar units** it is simpler still. For the Earth around the Sun, $a =
1\ \mathrm{AU}$, $P = 1\ \mathrm{yr}$ and $M = 1\,M_\odot$, so dividing
@eq-kepler-mass by the same formula for the Earth cancels the $4\pi^2/G$ and
leaves

$$
\frac{M}{M_\odot} = \frac{\left(a/1\ \mathrm{AU}\right)^3}{\left(P/1\ \mathrm{yr}\right)^2} ,
$$ {#eq-kepler-solar}

the second form on your constants sheet: **the cube of the orbit in
astronomical units, over the square of the period in years, is the mass in
solar masses.**

**What is actually measured** is an angle, not a length. The semi-major axis
comes from its size on the sky, $\theta$, and the distance $d$, through
@eq-small-angle, $a = \theta d$, so

$$
M = \frac{4\pi^2\,\theta^3\, d^3}{G\,P^2} \propto d^{3} .
$$

**The mass depends on the cube of the distance.** A distance 3% too small
gives a mass 9% too small. The way out is the star's spectrum. The Doppler
shift of S2's lines (lecture 3) gives its speed toward or away from us in
kilometers per second, while its motion across the sky gives the same orbit's
speed in arcseconds per year, and the orbit has to make both agree. The ratio
of a speed in kilometers per second to the same speed in arcseconds per year
is a distance. So **S2 measures the distance to the Galactic center as well
as the mass there**, and the published fits give both together: $M =
4.30 \times 10^{6}\,M_\odot$ at $d = 8.28\ \mathrm{kpc}$ [@gravity2022mass].

### Numerical exploration

@fig-kepler plots @eq-kepler-solar: the period of an orbit against its size,
for a central mass of one Sun and for the four million solar masses of
Sgr A\*, on logarithmic axes, where each is a straight line. The planets sit
on the Sun's line. S2 sits on the other, a thousand times farther out than the
Earth and only sixteen times slower.

```{python}
#| label: fig-kepler
#| fig-cap: "Kepler's third law, $P^2 = a^3/M$ in years, astronomical units and solar masses (@eq-kepler-solar), for a central mass of $1\\,M_\\odot$ (the Sun) and of $4.3 \\times 10^{6}\\,M_\\odot$ (Sgr A\\*), on logarithmic axes. The planets Earth, Jupiter and Neptune lie on the Sun's line; the star S2 lies on Sgr A\\*'s. A larger mass shifts the whole line down: the same orbit, gone around faster."
#| fig-alt: "A chart with logarithmic axes. The horizontal axis is the semi-major axis of an orbit, from 0.3 to 3000 astronomical units, and the vertical axis is the orbital period, from 0.001 to 100,000 years. Two parallel straight lines rise from lower left to upper right. The upper one, in orange, is labeled 1 solar mass, the Sun; orange dots for Earth at 1 AU and 1 year, Jupiter at 5.2 AU and 12 years, and Neptune at 30 AU and 165 years sit on it. The lower line, in blue, is labeled 4.3 million solar masses, Sgr A star, and lies more than three powers of ten below. A green dot for the star S2 sits on the blue line at about 1000 AU and 16 years, directly below where the orange line would put a period of about 32,000 years."
#| fig-height: 4.4

# The star to put on the plot: its semi-major axis in AU and period in years.
a_star = 1004.0        # semi-major axis of the star's orbit, in AU
P_star = 16.05         # period of the star's orbit, in years

a = np.logspace(np.log10(0.3), np.log10(3000), 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 4.4))
for M, color, label, xy in ((1.0, ORANGE, r"$1\,M_\odot$, the Sun", (0.45, 2.0)),
                            (4.3e6, BLUE, r"$4.3 \times 10^{6}\,M_\odot$, Sgr A*",
                             (12, 3.0e-3))):
    ax.plot(a, np.sqrt(a**3 / M), color=color, lw=2)
    ax.text(*xy, label, color=color, fontsize=10.5, rotation=27,
            rotation_mode="anchor")
for name, ap, Pp in (("Earth", 1.0, 1.0), ("Jupiter", 5.2, 11.9),
                     ("Neptune", 30.1, 164.8)):
    ax.plot([ap], [Pp], "o", color=ORANGE, ms=6, mec=INK, mew=0.6, zorder=3)
    ax.text(ap * 1.25, Pp / 1.6, name, color=INK2, fontsize=9.5)
M_star = a_star**3 / P_star**2
ax.plot([a_star], [P_star], "o", color=AQUA, ms=8, mec=INK, mew=0.8, zorder=4)
ax.text(a_star / 1.3, P_star * 1.8, "the star", color=INK2, fontsize=9.5,
        ha="right")
print(f"a = {a_star:g} AU, P = {P_star:g} yr: M = a^3/P^2 = {M_star:.3g} Msun")
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(0.3, 3000)
ax.set_ylim(1e-3, 1e5)
ax.set_xlabel(r"semi-major axis, $a$ (AU)")
ax.set_ylabel(r"period, $P$ (years)")
plt.show()
```

```{pyodide}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 4.4))
for M, color, label, xy in ((1.0, ORANGE, r"$1\,M_\odot$, the Sun", (0.45, 2.0)),
                            (4.3e6, BLUE, r"$4.3 \times 10^{6}\,M_\odot$, Sgr A*",
                             (12, 3.0e-3))):
    ax.plot(a, np.sqrt(a**3 / M), color=color, lw=2)
    ax.text(*xy, label, color=color, fontsize=10.5, rotation=27,
            rotation_mode="anchor")
for name, ap, Pp in (("Earth", 1.0, 1.0), ("Jupiter", 5.2, 11.9),
                     ("Neptune", 30.1, 164.8)):
    ax.plot([ap], [Pp], "o", color=ORANGE, ms=6, mec=INK, mew=0.6, zorder=3)
    ax.text(ap * 1.25, Pp / 1.6, name, color=INK2, fontsize=9.5)
M_star = a_star**3 / P_star**2
ax.plot([a_star], [P_star], "o", color=AQUA, ms=8, mec=INK, mew=0.8, zorder=4)
ax.text(a_star / 1.3, P_star * 1.8, "the star", color=INK2, fontsize=9.5,
        ha="right")
print(f"a = {a_star:g} AU, P = {P_star:g} yr: M = a^3/P^2 = {M_star:.3g} Msun")
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(0.3, 3000)
ax.set_ylim(1e-3, 1e5)
ax.set_xlabel(r"semi-major axis, $a$ (AU)")
ax.set_ylabel(r"period, $P$ (years)")
plt.show()
```
:::

:::

::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: weighing Sgr A* with S2"}
**The question.** S2's orbit has a semi-major axis of $1004\ \mathrm{AU}$ at a
distance of $8.0\ \mathrm{kpc}$ (the first worked example) and a period of
$16.05$ years. What is the mass of Sgr A\*, in solar masses?

The solar-unit form of Kepler's law, @eq-kepler-solar, needs only the cube of
one number and the square of another. Keep the units on:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{M}{M_\odot} &= \frac{\left(1004\ \mathrm{AU} / 1\ \mathrm{AU}\right)^3}
                         {\left(16.05\ \mathrm{yr} / 1\ \mathrm{yr}\right)^2} \\[0.8em]
                  &= \frac{1.012 \times 10^{9}}{257.6} .
\end{aligned}
$$

The astronomical units cancel on top and the years on the bottom, so the ratio
is a pure number, and it is the mass in solar masses. *Do the units make
sense?* A mass in units of the Sun's, so yes. The numbers give

$$
M = 3.9 \times 10^{6}\,M_\odot .
$$

**Four million solar masses.** The published value is
$4.30 \times 10^{6}\,M_\odot$ [@gravity2022mass], about 9% larger, and the
difference is the distance: the same fit puts the Galactic center at
$8.28\ \mathrm{kpc}$, 3.5% farther than the $8.0\ \mathrm{kpc}$ we used, and
the mass goes as the cube of the distance, $1.035^{3} = 1.11$.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-weighing}

1. Check @eq-kepler-solar against Jupiter, which orbits the Sun at
   $5.20\ \mathrm{AU}$ every $11.86$ years. What mass does it give for the
   Sun?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   It gives $5.20^3 / 11.86^2 = 140.6/140.7 = 1.00\,M_\odot$.
   :::

2. The star S4716 orbits Sgr A\* every 4.02 years on an orbit with a
   semi-major axis of 402 AU [@peissker2022]. What mass does it give for
   Sgr A\*?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   It gives $402^3/4.02^2 = 4.0 \times 10^{6}\,M_\odot$, the same as S2 gives.
   :::

3. Suppose the distance to the Galactic center were $8.3\ \mathrm{kpc}$
   instead of $8.0$, with the angles and the period unchanged. By what factor
   would every mass measured from the stars' orbits change? Would the
   measured *periods* change?

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
   The semi-major axis in AU is the angle times the distance, and the mass goes
   as its cube. The period is measured with a clock, and does not depend on
   the distance at all.

   The masses would all be $(8.3/8.0)^3 = 1.12$ times larger, 12% more. The
   periods would not change.
   :::

4. A star at the Galactic center moves across the sky by $0.026''$ per year,
   and its speed across the sky is known (from the shape of its orbit and the
   Doppler shift of its lines) to be $1000\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. How far away
   is it, in parsecs?

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
   Turn the speed into astronomical units per year. In one year the star moves
   a distance $s$ in AU, which spans $0.026''$, and @eq-small-angle then gives
   the distance in parsecs.

   A speed of $1000\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ is $211\ \mathrm{AU}$ per year, so the distance
   is $211/0.026 = 8100\ \mathrm{pc}$, about $8.1\ \mathrm{kpc}$.
   :::

5. A planet orbits a star at $2\ \mathrm{AU}$ every 1.41 years. What is the
   mass of the star? Now suppose the same planet were moved to S2's
   semi-major axis, about $1000\ \mathrm{AU}$, around the same star. How long
   would one orbit take?

:::

## Why it must be a black hole

Four million solar masses, then. The next question is how small a space they
fit in, and the answer comes from S2's closest approach. At pericenter the
star passes about $120\ \mathrm{AU}$ from Sgr A\*, seventeen light-hours,
three times the size of Neptune's orbit, and its orbit there is still the
ellipse that four million solar masses at a point would give. **The whole mass
is inside $120\ \mathrm{AU}$.** For a mass that large, that is very small: the
Schwarzschild radius of $4.3 \times 10^{6}\,M_\odot$ is
$1.3 \times 10^{12}\ \mathrm{cm}$, $0.085\ \mathrm{AU}$, and S2's closest
approach is still more than a thousand times larger. What could be in there?

**Not ordinary stars.** Four million Suns spread through a sphere
$120\ \mathrm{AU}$ in radius would be about one astronomical unit apart, and
they would be in plain sight: four million suns, all within a fraction of an
arcsecond, would outshine everything around them. Nothing like that is seen.

**Not a cluster of dark objects either.** Suppose the mass were white dwarfs,
neutron stars or stellar-mass black holes, dark but packed just as tightly. A
cluster that dense would not last. Its members would pass close to one another
again and again, some would be flung out and the rest would sink to the
center, and in far less time than the age of the Galaxy the cluster would have
evaporated or collapsed; collapse leaves one black hole
[@maoz1998; @schodel2002; @genzel2010].

**And the center sits still.** Sgr A\*, the radio source, is not moving: it
stays at the focus of every orbit, and its motion out of the plane of the Galaxy is under two kilometers per
second [@reid2020]. Something light would be jostled by the stars around it,
at speeds like theirs; to stay that still, the radio source must itself carry
at least about a quarter of the four million solar masses. The mass is *in*
the radio source, not merely near it.

Lecture 16 added the last piece. The Event Horizon Telescope's picture of Sgr
A\* is a ring of light around a dark center, at the size general relativity
predicts for a black hole of exactly the mass the stars give
[@eht2022sgra]. Two methods, one with starlight and one with radio waves, one
blind to light bending and one built on it, agree.

**And it is very quiet.** A black hole of four million solar masses has an
Eddington luminosity (lecture 8) of $5 \times 10^{44}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$,
over a hundred billion Suns, enough to make it a respectable quasar.
Sgr A\* gives off about three billionths of that: averaged over time it
shines more than eight powers of ten below its Eddington limit
[@genzel2010], a few hundred times the Sun's luminosity, from an object
that could outshine its whole galaxy. It is the kind of dead quasar that Lynden-Bell
predicted would sit in every galaxy (lecture 18): a black hole that grew long
ago and is now starved of gas.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-black-hole}

1. How many Schwarzschild radii of a $4.3 \times 10^{6}\,M_\odot$ black hole
   is S2's closest approach, $120\ \mathrm{AU}$?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   The Schwarzschild radius is $1.27 \times 10^{12}\ \mathrm{cm} =
   0.085\ \mathrm{AU}$, so $120\ \mathrm{AU}$ is about 1400 Schwarzschild
   radii.
   :::

2. Suppose the four million solar masses inside S2's closest approach were
   four million Suns, spread evenly through a sphere $120\ \mathrm{AU}$ in
   radius. About how far apart would neighboring stars be? Compare with the
   size of the Sun, $7 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm}$.

3. Use the Eddington luminosity from lecture 8 to find the most luminous Sgr
   A\* could be while feeding steadily, in solar luminosities.
   Averaged over time, Sgr A\* shines at about $10^{-8.5}$ of that
   [@genzel2010]. How many Suns' worth of light is that?

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
   Use $L_{\mathrm{Edd}} \approx 1.26 \times 10^{38}\,(M/M_\odot)\
   \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$, and the Sun's luminosity is on your constants sheet.

   The Eddington luminosity is $L_{\mathrm{Edd}} = 5.4 \times 10^{44}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}} = 1.4 \times
   10^{11}\,L_\odot$, and $10^{-8.5}$ of it is about 450 Suns.
   :::

:::

## Two tests of general relativity

S2 is useful twice over. Its orbit weighs Sgr A\*, and at its closest approach
it is deep enough in the black hole's gravity that the corrections general
relativity makes to Newton's picture become large enough to measure. Lecture 4
met one of them, the precession of an orbit, and lecture 5 the other, the
redshift of light climbing out of a gravitational field. Here is how big each
one is for S2.

**How big.** Both effects are controlled by one ratio: how close the star
comes, in units of the Schwarzschild radius, $r_S/r$. For a body falling around
a mass, it is also, roughly, the square of its speed in units of the speed of
light, since the Newtonian speed of an orbit at distance $r$ satisfies
$v^2 \sim GM/r = \tfrac12 r_S c^2/r$:

$$
\beta^2 = \frac{v^2}{c^2} \sim \frac{r_S}{r} .
$$ {#eq-beta2}

For the Earth around the Sun it is $10^{-8}$, and general relativity's
corrections to the Earth's orbit are that small. For S2 at closest approach
it is nearly $10^{-3}$, a hundred thousand times larger.

::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: how big are the relativistic effects for S2?"}
**The question.** S2 passes $17$ light-hours from Sgr A\*, whose mass is
$4.3 \times 10^{6}\,M_\odot$. What is $r_S/r$ there, and how fast a speed, in
kilometers per second, is that fraction of the speed of light?

The Schwarzschild radius, with $M = 4.3 \times 10^{6} \times 1.9891 \times
10^{33}\ \mathrm{g} = 8.55 \times 10^{39}\ \mathrm{g}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
r_S &= \frac{2GM}{c^2} \\[0.8em]
    &= \frac{2 \times 6.6732 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm^{3}\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}}
                     \times 8.55 \times 10^{39}\ \mathrm{g}}
                    {\left(2.998 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\right)^2} \\[0.8em]
     &= 1.27 \times 10^{12}\ \mathrm{cm} .
\end{aligned}
$$

The grams cancel and $\mathrm{cm^{3}\,s^{-2}}$ over $\mathrm{cm^{2}\,s^{-2}}$
leaves centimeters. *Do the units make sense?* A radius, so yes. The distance
is light's speed times 17 hours:

$$
\begin{aligned}
r &= 2.998 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}} \times 17\ \mathrm{h}
     \times \frac{3600\ \mathrm{s}}{1\ \mathrm{h}} \\[0.8em]
  &= 1.83 \times 10^{15}\ \mathrm{cm} .
\end{aligned}
$$

So

$$
\frac{r_S}{r} = \frac{1.27 \times 10^{12}\ \mathrm{cm}}{1.83 \times 10^{15}\ \mathrm{cm}}
             = 6.9 \times 10^{-4} ,
$$

a pure number, as a ratio of two lengths must be. As a speed,

$$
6.9 \times 10^{-4} \times 3.00 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}
  = 210\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}} .
$$

**About seven parts in ten thousand, or two hundred kilometers per second.**
S2's ordinary Doppler shift at closest approach swings by thousands of
kilometers per second, so the relativistic part is a few percent of it:
small, but well within reach of a good spectrograph.
:::

### The redshift

Light from S2 reaches us redshifted for three reasons. The first is the plain
Doppler shift of its motion along our line of sight, lecture 3's, which
Newton's orbit predicts exactly and which swings by thousands of kilometers per
second as the star rounds the black hole. The other two are the ones
relativity adds, and each is about half of @eq-beta2:

* **The moving clock runs slow.** S2's atoms are clocks moving at a few
  percent of the speed of light, and time dilation (lecture 3) makes them tick
  slow by a fraction $\gamma - 1 \approx \tfrac12 v^2/c^2$, whichever way the
  star is moving. This is the *transverse Doppler effect*, and it always
  reddens the light.
* **The light climbs out of the black hole's gravity.** From lecture 5, light
  emitted at distance $r$ from a mass arrives redshifted by
  $z \approx GM/rc^2 = \tfrac12 r_S/r$ when $r \gg r_S$.

Together they redden S2's light at closest approach by about $200\
\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, on top of a Doppler swing of thousands
(@fig-s2-redshift). In 2018 GRAVITY followed S2 through closest approach and
measured exactly this extra redshift: as a fraction of what general relativity
predicts, they found $f = 0.90 \pm 0.09$, with a further $\pm 0.15$ of
systematic uncertainty, where $f = 0$ would mean Newton and
$f = 1$ Einstein [@gravity2018redshift]. The UCLA group, with the Keck telescopes,
measured the same thing independently a year later, $0.88 \pm 0.17$ on the
same scale [@do2019].

```{python}
#| label: fig-s2-redshift
#| fig-cap: "The radial velocity of S2, computed from the orbit fitted by the GRAVITY Collaboration [@gravity2020precession]. Top: the ordinary Doppler velocity of Newton's orbit, positive when the star moves away from us, from 2000 to 2022. It drifts slowly for most of the orbit and swings by thousands of kilometers per second in a few months around each closest approach, in 2002 and 2018. Bottom: what general relativity adds, the transverse Doppler shift and the gravitational redshift together, around the 2018 approach. It is under $30\\ \\mathrm{km\\,s^{-1}}$ for most of the orbit and peaks at about $200\\ \\mathrm{km\\,s^{-1}}$ at closest approach. This is a model, not data; the deck shows the measurements, which follow the bottom curve."
#| fig-alt: "Two charts stacked, sharing a time axis in years. The top chart shows radial velocity in kilometers per second from 2000 to 2022: a blue curve that climbs slowly from about minus 1500 to plus 2000 over most of the period, with a sudden swing in 2002 and again in 2018, each rising steeply to about plus 4000 and then plunging to about minus 2000 within a few months. The bottom chart, from 2014 to 2022, shows the extra redshift from relativity in kilometers per second, as an orange curve that stays near 10 to 30 kilometers per second, rises sharply to a peak of about 200 in 2018, and falls back. A dotted vertical line marks the 2018 closest approach in both charts."
#| fig-height: 5.0

t = np.linspace(2000.0, 2022.0, 6000)
_, _, r, speed, v_r = s2_state(t)
z_rel = 0.5 * speed**2 / C**2 + G * S2["M"] * MSUN / (r * C**2)
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(5.8, 5.0), sharex=False,
                               gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1.15, 1]))
ax1.plot(t, v_r / KMS, color=BLUE, lw=1.8)
ax1.axhline(0, color=AXIS, lw=0.8, zorder=0)
ax1.set_xlim(2000, 2022)
ax1.set_xticks([2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020])
ax1.set_ylabel(r"Doppler velocity (km s$^{-1}$)")
tz = t[(t > 2014) & (t < 2022)]
_, _, rz, sz, _ = s2_state(tz)
zz = 0.5 * sz**2 / C**2 + G * S2["M"] * MSUN / (rz * C**2)
ax2.plot(tz, zz * C / KMS, color=ORANGE, lw=2)
ax2.set_xlim(2014, 2022)
ax2.set_ylim(0, 240)
ax2.set_xlabel("year")
ax2.set_ylabel(r"relativistic redshift (km s$^{-1}$)")
for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    ax.axvline(S2["tp"], color=MUTED, lw=1, ls=":", zorder=0)
ax2.text(S2["tp"] + 0.25, 200, "closest\napproach", color=INK2, fontsize=9.5,
         va="top")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### The precession

Lecture 4 gave the angle by which an orbit's long axis turns each time
around, in curved spacetime:

$$
\Delta\phi = \frac{3\pi\, r_S}{a\,(1 - e^2)} ,
$$ {#eq-precession}

where $a$ is the semi-major axis and $e$ the eccentricity. For S2, with $a =
1031\ \mathrm{AU}$, $e = 0.885$ and $M = 4.26 \times 10^{6}\,M_\odot$, it is
$3.5 \times 10^{-3}$ radians per orbit, **about twelve arcminutes**, the number lecture 4 quoted. Mercury's
is a tenth of an arcsecond per orbit; S2's is seven thousand times larger.

Twelve arcminutes is a big angle, but seen from Earth it is a tiny shift. The
orbit turns about Sgr A\*, so a point a distance $r$ from it moves sideways by
about $r\,\Delta\phi$. At closest approach that is half an astronomical unit;
at the far end of the orbit, almost two thousand astronomical units out, it is
about seven, under a thousandth of an arcsecond. It took GRAVITY's sharpness,
and S2's passage through closest approach in 2018, to see it. In 2020 the
GRAVITY Collaboration reported the precession at $f_{\mathrm{SP}} =
1.10 \pm 0.19$ times general relativity's prediction [@gravity2020precession]: S2's orbit is
not a closed ellipse but a slowly turning rosette, as Einstein's theory says.

::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Think about why both tests had to wait for closest approach"}
Both effects scale as $r_S/r$. S2's orbit has $e = 0.885$, so its farthest
point is $(1 + e)/(1 - e) = 16$ times farther from Sgr A\* than its closest,
and the relativistic redshift there is thirty times smaller, about seven
kilometers per second. Most of the redshift, and most of the precession's
turning, happens in the few months around closest approach (the bottom panel
of @fig-s2-redshift). And those months are exactly when the ordinary Doppler
shift changes fastest, so the Newtonian orbit has to be known extremely well
to be subtracted. That is why it took two closest approaches, sixteen years
apart, and a new instrument for the second, to make the measurement.
:::

<!-- american-spelling: ignore-begin
     The Nobel motivation is quoted verbatim, in the committee's spelling. -->
Andrea Ghez and Reinhard Genzel shared half of the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics
for this work, *"for the discovery of a supermassive compact object at
the centre of our galaxy"* [@nobel2020]. The other half went to Roger
Penrose, for showing that general relativity predicts black holes form.
<!-- american-spelling: ignore-end -->

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

## If you want to go further

**The papers.** The GRAVITY Collaboration's two letters on the redshift
[-@gravity2018redshift] and the precession [-@gravity2020precession] are each a few pages, and
their figures are the ones in the lecture slides. The review by Genzel,
Eisenhauer and Gillessen [-@genzel2010] tells the whole story of the Galactic
center up to 2010 at length.

**The closest stars.** S2 is no longer the star with the shortest known
period: S4716 goes around Sgr A\* in about four years [@peissker2022]. Stars
on still smaller orbits would feel the black hole's spin (lecture 2), and
finding one is a goal of the next generation of telescopes.

## Summary

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| Where | Sgr A\*, $8.0\ \mathrm{kpc}$ away; one arcsecond is 8000 AU there | seen in the infrared, with adaptive optics and interferometry |
| The star | S2: a 16-year orbit, $\sim 1000\ \mathrm{AU}$ across, closest approach $120\ \mathrm{AU}$ | followed all the way around, twice |
| The mass | $M = 4\pi^2 a^3/GP^2$, or $a^3/P^2$ in AU, years and $M_\odot$ | about $4.3 \times 10^{6}\,M_\odot$, and the distance too |
| Why a black hole | four million $M_\odot$ inside $120\ \mathrm{AU}$, at rest, the right size for the EHT | no cluster of stars could survive that dense |
| How quiet | far below its Eddington luminosity | a starved, dead quasar |
| Redshift | time dilation and gravitational redshift, each $\tfrac12 r_S/r$ | $\sim 200\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ at closest approach, measured 2018 |
| Precession | $\Delta\phi = 3\pi r_S/a(1 - e^2)$ | twelve arcminutes an orbit, measured 2020 |

The black hole at the center of the Milky Way is the best-weighed black hole in
the universe, and it is quiet. Next time we look at the ones that are not:
the active galactic nuclei, of which the quasars of lecture 18 are the
brightest, and the one picture, seen from different angles, that explains them
all.
